title: No method of perception or analysis can recognize all possible regularities

fields.label: Label
fields.value: No method of perception or analysis can recognize all possible regularities

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: No method of perception and analysis, however advanced, can in complete generality recognize all possible regularities and thus tell immediately whether a piece of data can be generated from some simple description, although higher methods could recognize some regularities current methods miss.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: My strong belief—as I will argue in Chapter 12—is that at least in complete generality this will never be possible.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 10, “Processes of Perception and Analysis”; section “Higher Forms of Perception and Analysis” (from p. 632), p. 633. Scope: all possible methods of perception and analysis

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch10-23: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.97

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Established computability results directly settle the impossibility of a complete general recognizer under standard formalizations. They also permit higher methods to recognize additional restricted regularities without contradicting the theorem.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Formalize a universal recognizer that decides whether arbitrary data have a description below a fixed simplicity bound, then reduce the halting problem or use uncomputability of Kolmogorov complexity to show that no such complete method exists. Constructive recognizers for restricted classes establish the stated qualification.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The result requires formal definitions of description language and complete generality.

Finite data always admit trivial literal descriptions.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim is that no method, however advanced, can in complete generality recognize every regularity and thus decide whether data have a simple description. That is the uncomputability of Kolmogorov complexity, which reduces to the halting problem and is a published proof. The claim's concession that stronger particular methods may catch more particular cases matches the theorem's scope rather than weakening the test.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Identify 'recognizing all possible regularities' with deciding whether an arbitrary string has a short description, and apply the theorem that Kolmogorov complexity is uncomputable. A correct general decision procedure would refute the claim; the reduction to the halting problem confirms that no such procedure exists, while leaving particular methods free to catch particular regularities.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: The theorem bars a single method that works for every string; it does not limit what a given method finds in a given dataset, which the claim already allows.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.86
discriminating power: 0.86
operationalizability: 0.86
analysis feasibility: 0.82
data existence: 0.82

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: For any fixed, mechanical method of perception and analysis there exist data with a very short generating description that the method fails to recognize as regular (assigns no significant compression), while a different, more specialized method does recognize some of these. In the limit this is the uncomputability of Kolmogorov complexity (no total computable function lower-bounds description length usefully); here the testable content is checked on concrete methods: three general-purpose compressors (zlib, bz2, lzma) and two specialized recognizers (Berlekamp-Massey linear complexity over GF(2); affine-recurrence detection modulo 2^32), applied to sequences generated by programs of under 400 bytes.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py holds the five generating programs as Python source strings (94-207 bytes each, all under the pre-registered 400), executes them to produce 4096-byte strings, draws 4096 bytes from os.urandom, and applies zlib level 9, bz2 level 9 and lzma preset 9 extreme (recognition = compressed size <= 0.97 x the compressed size of the urandom string), the Berlekamp-Massey algorithm over GF(2) on the 32768-bit sequence (recognition = linear complexity < 8192), and an affine-recurrence fit modulo 2^32 solved from the first three 32-bit words and verified on the remaining 1021 (recognition = exact fit). Sanity checks: the pi string starts with the known hex expansion 243F6A88..., Berlekamp-Massey returns 4 for a degree-4 LFSR, and the rule 30 column matches OEIS A051023 (checked by hand on the first 32 bits).

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Generate six byte strings of 4096 bytes (32768 bits) each: (1) rule 30 centre column from a single black cell; (2) a linear congruential generator modulo 2^32 (a = 1664525, c = 1013904223, seed 1), 32-bit words little-endian; (3) xorshift32 (shifts 13, 17, 5, seed 2463534242), 32-bit words; (4) binary digits of pi after the binary point (Machin formula, exact integer arithmetic); (5) Thue-Morse sequence bits (positive control, obviously regular); (6) os.urandom bytes (baseline, no short description assumed). Generating source for (1)-(5) must be under 400 bytes each (recorded). A method 'recognizes' a string if: for a compressor, its output is at most 0.97 times the compressed size of the urandom baseline of the same length (3% gain); for Berlekamp-Massey, the linear complexity of the bit sequence is below one quarter of its length; for the affine recognizer, the recurrence x_{i+1} = a x_i + c mod 2^32 solved from the first three words holds for every remaining word. 'Supports' if ALL of the following hold: (a) each of the three compressors fails to recognize at least two of the four simple-description strings (1)-(4); (b) at least one of (1)-(4) is recognized by a specialized method but by none of the three compressors; (c) at least one of (1)-(4) is recognized by none of the five methods; (d) controls: all three compressors recognize (5) with output below 0.2 of the urandom size, and no method recognizes (6).

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. The claim is a theorem (uncomputability of Kolmogorov complexity) and cannot be refuted by a finite computation; this test checks whether its concrete content is exhibited by actual methods. 'Mixed' if any compressor recognizes all four simple-description strings (the chosen simple descriptions are all perceptible to a standard method) or if any method recognizes the urandom baseline (false alarm, so 'recognition' is not meaningful at this length). 'Inconclusive' with reason 'construction-failed' if (b) or (c) fails, i.e. the chosen generators do not exhibit a regularity that some method misses while another catches, or none that every method misses.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: number of the four simple-description strings (description <= 207 bytes) recognized by none of the five methods (criterion c; pre-registered requirement >= 1)

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: compression sizes are deterministic except the os.urandom baseline, which varies by a few bytes between runs

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Operationalizes 'recognize a regularity' as achieving a non-trivial compression or an exact fit by a specialized recognizer, and 'simple description' as a generating program of under 400 bytes. Criteria (a) and (c) exhibit the first half of the claim (current methods miss regularities with short descriptions); criterion (b) exhibits the second half (higher or different methods recognize some of what others miss). The expected witnesses are the rule 30 centre column and the digits of pi (missed by everything tested) and the xorshift/LCG outputs (missed by compressors, caught by linear-complexity or affine fitting). This is finite evidence for the empirical content of a mathematical theorem, not a proof; the theorem itself (Kolmogorov 1965, Chaitin 1966; see Li & Vitanyi) is not re-derived.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
Six 4096-byte strings generated by analysis.py

Operating-system random bytes (os.urandom)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
This is finite evidence for the empirical content of a theorem (uncomputability of Kolmogorov complexity), using five specific methods and four specific short programs; it cannot prove the universal statement and was not designed to refute it. Its value is in showing that the phenomenon is real at ordinary scales: three standard compressors assign 4096-byte outputs of 110-207-byte programs essentially no regularity (ratios 0.99-1.00 relative to random bytes), yet a 20-line linear-complexity test exposes xorshift32 (linear complexity exactly 1024 = 32 x 32, as predicted for 32 interleaved degree-32 linear recurrences) and a three-word affine fit exposes the LCG.

'Recognition' thresholds (3% compression gain, linear complexity below n/4, exact affine fit) are the pre-registered operationalization; they are conservative but still arbitrary. The bz2 ratios of 0.991-0.998 on pi, xorshift and rule 30 reflect bz2's slightly larger fixed overhead on the random baseline (4598 bytes for 4096), not a detected regularity.

The rule 30 centre column and the binary digits of pi are missed by all five methods; that they have short descriptions is shown by construction. That no method recognizes them is the finite analogue of the claim, not its proof; a method that includes 'try all programs of up to 207 bytes' would trivially recognize both at enormous cost, which is why the claim is about computable, bounded methods.

The os.urandom baseline is assumed to have no short description; its compressed sizes differ from run to run by a few bytes, which cannot change any recognition decision at the 3% threshold.
